item.text: {"question_id":"3B.3","answer":"The record is mixed. Tshisekedi publicly promoted love, unity, equality, and opposition to divisiveness, and stated that Congolese law prohibited and sanctioned tribal, ethnic, racial, and xenophobic hate speech (BATCH-0020-E015; BATCH-0016-E003). However, he also said he would target without hesitation or regret people he considered threats to national security and stability, warned that foreigners would manufacture candidates, and used strongly hostile language toward Rwanda and M23. The Rwanda/M23 rhetoric concerned an external armed conflict and is contextual here unless a domestic targeting or harm chain is established (BATCH-0003-E010; BATCH-0018-E007; BATCH-0007-E013). Domestic campaign-period evidence raises a more substantial concern about the conduct of aligned officials and supporters: CSAC found that a UDPS provincial governor’s statement incited ethnic-regional hatred, exclusion, and discrimination; ACLED recorded UDPS supporters as both the most targeted group and the most active in violence against other political groups since 2019; and Human Rights Watch reported UDPS-linked attacks in Kasumbalesa that injured six people, involved rape and sexual assault, and were not known to have been investigated (BATCH-0002-E017; BATCH-0010-E021; BATCH-0002-E014). The 2023 human-rights assessment likewise recorded hate speech, violence or threats against journalists and ethnic groups, security-force abuses, and persistent impunity, while also noting some investigations and punishment of officials; it does not establish that Tshisekedi personally directed or endorsed each abuse (BATCH-0011-E008). Thus, the evidence supports concern about hostile presidential security rhetoric, an insufficiently controlled ruling-party environment, and weak or undocumented remedy after reported harm, but does not prove a personal presidential incitement-to-violence chain or establish that external-conflict rhetoric itself constituted domestic
